note.explanation: Hydrocarbons contain carbon and hydrogen only. Carbon can form strong covalent bonds with itself, so it can make long chains, branched chains and rings. Many fuels are hydrocarbons, and they are also used to make other useful compounds.
examples: Natural gas is a fuel made mainly of hydrocarbons.
Methane is the simplest alkane and has the formula CH₄.
note.checkAnswer: Hydrocarbons are compounds containing carbon and hydrogen only.
note.simple: A hydrocarbon is a compound made only from carbon and hydrogen atoms.
note.title: Hydrocarbons: carbon and hydrogen
steps: Check which elements are present in the compound.
If it contains only carbon and hydrogen, it is a hydrocarbon.
Remember that carbon can join to other carbon atoms to form chains and rings.

written.finalAnswer: A structural formula shows the symbols for the atoms present in a compound connected by short lines which represent the bonds present in it.

written.text: Differentiate between an organic and an inorganic compound.
written.finalAnswer: Organic compounds are carbon compounds, usually containing hydrogen as well; carbonates, cyanides, carbides, cyanates and oxides of carbon are classified as inorganic compounds.

written.text: Why are organic compounds found in large numbers?
written.finalAnswer: Carbon forms four covalent bonds and can bond strongly with itself; its self-linking property, called catenation, enables it to form long, straight and branched chains and rings.

rubric.why: Carbon's bonding ability explains why it can form many different compounds.
rubric.description: States that carbon forms four covalent bonds and/or has catenation.
rubric.how: Mention carbon's four covalent bonds or its self-linking property.

rubric.why: Different carbon frameworks lead to the great variety of organic compounds.
rubric.description: Explains that carbon forms chains, branches or rings.
rubric.how: Connect catenation to the different structures carbon can make.

modelAnswer: Carbon forms four covalent bonds and forms strong, stable bonds with itself.
The self-linking property of carbon is called catenation.
Due to catenation, carbon forms long, straight and branched chains and rings.
This gives rise to a very large number of organic compounds.

written.text: How are organic compounds useful for us?
written.finalAnswer: Organic compounds include biomolecules, pharmaceuticals and synthetic fibres; hydrocarbons are used as fuels and as feedstock for plastics, medicines, synthetic fibres, paints and varnishes.

written.text: Why is carbon so important as an element that the whole branch of chemistry is based on it?
written.finalAnswer: Carbon forms four covalent bonds, makes strong and stable bonds with itself and other elements, and shows catenation; it can therefore form many long, straight and branched chains and rings, producing a very large number of compounds.

modelAnswer: Carbon is generally unable to gain or lose electrons to form ionic bonds, so it forms four covalent bonds.
Because of its small size, these covalent bonds are short and strong.
Carbon forms strong, stable bonds with itself and with hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen.
The self-linking property of carbon is called catenation.
Catenation enables carbon to form long, straight and branched chains and rings.
These properties allow carbon to form a very large number of compounds.

written.text: Describe the importance of organic compounds in daily life.
written.finalAnswer: Organic compounds are important as biomolecules, fuels and pharmaceuticals, and they provide materials for products such as plastics, medicines, synthetic fibres, paints and varnishes.

explain.title: What are hydrocarbons?
explain.body: The family of hydrocarbons constitutes a very large number of simple organic compounds containing carbon and hydrogen only. This means that a hydrocarbon has carbon and hydrogen atoms and no other elements.

explain.title: Why can carbon make so many compounds?
explain.body: Carbon forms four covalent bonds. Its ability to link to itself is called catenation. Carbon can therefore form long, straight and branched chains and rings, which gives many possible structures.

explain.title: Structural formula and condensed form
explain.body: A structural formula shows the symbols for the atoms present in the compounds connected by short lines which represent the bonds present in them. For methane, the condensed form is CH₄.

explain.title: Why are hydrocarbons useful?
explain.body: Natural gas, LPG, CNG, petrol, diesel and kerosene oil are examples of everyday fuels identified as simple hydrocarbons. Hydrocarbons also serve as feedstock to prepare useful compounds such as plastics, medicines, synthetic fibres, paints and varnishes.

mistakes: Do not define a hydrocarbon as a compound containing carbon only; it contains carbon and hydrogen only.
Do not confuse a structural formula with a condensed or molecular formula: the structural formula shows bonds with short lines.
Do not say that catenation means carbon bonds only with hydrogen; it means carbon links to itself.
When explaining carbon's importance, do not leave out the link between catenation and the formation of chains and rings.
Do not list fuels as the only use of hydrocarbons; the section also describes their use as feedstock.
